title: Runtime Extension and Observability Integration Handbook
author: Aisha Khan
content:
Summary

This handbook defines the extension/plugin model and the associated observability and benchmarking contracts for Redwood's serving runtime. It is intended for runtime engineers, plugin authors (internal and partner vendors), SREs, and Performance Engineers who integrate custom kernels, pre/post-processing hooks, or telemetry exporters with the serving runtime. The goal is to provide a stable, low-friction integration surface while preserving runtime SLOs and operational observability.

Audience and scope
- Primary audience: eng-serving-runtime, eng-sre, and applied-ml teams.
- Scope: plugin lifecycle, API/telemetry contracts, recommended profiling hooks, benchmark integration, safe rollout checklist, and runbooks for extension-related incidents.

Design goals
- Safety-first: extensions must not violate memory or latency SLOs.
- Observable: every extension must expose standard telemetry and traces.
- Deterministic lifecycle: load/unload, canary, and rollback paths are explicitly defined.
- Low-onramp: standard manifests and a reference SDK accelerate partner integrations.

High-level architecture and key services referenced
- runtime-orchestrator: controls placement and lifecycle of model shards and extensions.
- kernel-scheduler-service: responsible for mapping requests to kernel implementations and enforcing priority/quotas.
- kv-cache-agent: shared KV prefix cache used by model sessions; extensions may read-only access via a guarded API.
- telemetry-pipeline: receives Prometheus metrics, OTLP traces, and logs (forwarded to internal observability stacks).
- perf-harness-runner: benchmark runner that executes synthetic and recorded traces against runtime variants.

Extension surface and lifecycle
1) Extension manifest (required fields)
   - name: unique identifier (namespace-qualified)
   - version: semver
   - type: kernel | preprocessor | postprocessor | telemetry-exporter
   - entrypoint: binary or module path
   - resources: cpu, gpu, memory soft/hard limits
   - capabilities: [kv_read, metrics, traces]

   Example (YAML manifest):

   name: redwood.ext.fast-attn
   version: 0.3.1
   type: kernel
   entrypoint: /opt/extensions/fast_attn.so
   resources:
     cpu: "2"
     gpu: "1"
     memory: "8Gi"
   capabilities: [kv_read, metrics, traces]

2) Load sequence
   - Orchestration: runtime-orchestrator validates manifest signature and resource claims, then schedules extension.
   - Warmup: extension must run a registration callback that reports supported kernel shapes and an internal readiness check (see API contract).
   - Activation: kernel-scheduler-service adds the extension to the routing table for compatible requests.

3) Unload sequence and safe rollback
   - New requests are drained within a configurable drain_window (default 30s).
   - Active requests are allowed to complete with a max_grace (default 120s).
   - Forced termination only with explicit operator approval and after emitting a decommission trace.

API and observability contract (required)
- Health and readiness endpoints: /healthz, /ready (HTTP 200/503 semantics).
- Registration RPC: RegisterExtension({shapes:[], capabilities:[]}) -> {success, diagnostics}. Called on startup and after hot-reload.
- Metrics: expose Prometheus-style metrics namespace: redwood_ext_<name>_*. All extensions must export the following metrics (names are exact):
  - redwood_ext_<name>_invocations_total (counter)
  - redwood_ext_<name>_invocation_errors_total (counter)
  - redwood_ext_<name>_processing_seconds_bucket (histogram)
  - redwood_ext_<name>_active_workers (gauge)

Standard metric SLOs and thresholds (enforced by SRE checks)
  - p95 processing latency for kernel extensions: < 50ms for small-shape requests (<=512 tokens), <150ms for long-shape requests (>=2048 tokens).
  - invocation error rate: < 0.1% sustained per 5 minute window.
  - active_workers: should not exceed the declared resources*2 without explicit autoscale approval.

Trace & span conventions
- All extension-related spans must use the following span.kind attributes: {span.kind: internal, ext.name: <name>, ext.version: <ver>, runtime.node: <node-id>}
- Must emit pre-kernel and post-kernel spans with attributes: request_id, tenant_id, model_name, token_count, kernel_shape_hint.
- Sampling: default 10% across normal traffic; can be increased to 100% for canaries (configurable via runtime-orchestrator).

Profiling hooks and kernel telemetry
- Extensions must implement lightweight event hooks for the following events: kernel_dispatch (include queue_size and priority), kernel_start (include occupancy_estimate), kernel_complete (include cycles, bytes_read, bytes_written), kernel_preempt (include preempt_reason).
- Recommended profiling context: when running the continuous profiler, the profiler must annotate samples with ext.name and kernel_hint to enable join with kernel-level traces.
- Kernel event JSON example (line-delimited in logs / OTLP):
{
  "ts": "2026-03-01T12:45:12.123Z",
  "event": "kernel_start",
  "ext": "redwood.ext.fast-attn",
  "node": "node-az1-07",
  "occupancy_estimate": 0.78,
  "queue_size": 3
}

Benchmarking integration (perf-harness-runner)
- Integration points: the extension manifests must include a benchmark_profile stanza describing synthetic shapes the perf-harness-runner can use.
- Profiles should map to: payloads (sequence lengths), concurrency shapes, and memory-budgeted allocation.
- Command example to run the reference profile: 
  perf-harness-runner --target runtime-orchestrator:443 --extension redwood.ext.fast-attn --profile small-seq-512 --duration 600s --out /tmp/bench-run.json

- Result schema (perf-harness-runner output): 
  - throughput_tokens_per_sec, latency_p50_ms, latency_p95_ms, memory_young_bytes, memory_total_bytes, kernel_evicts

- Performance gate: a reference kernel extension must meet baseline envelope for green canary: latency_p95 <= baseline_p95 * 1.15 and memory_total_bytes <= baseline_memory * 1.20. Failure blocks automated canary promotion.

Rollout and canary checklist
1) Manifest signed and uploaded to extension-registry (owner: eng-serving-runtime)
2) Run unit and integration tests (CI job: ext-ci/fast-attn)
3) Run perf-harness-runner against a dev cluster; collect metrics and traces
4) Canary to 1% traffic for 30 minutes; sample traces at 100% for canary window
5) Evaluate SLOs: p95 latency, invocation error rate, scheduler queue length, KV cache hit behavior
6) Promote to 10% for 2 hours; run full benchmark profile
7) Full rollout after passing automated gates and manual review by SRE and runtime lead

Runbook: Extension-induced latency regression
- Symptoms:
  - sudden p95 spike for model routes pinned to new kernel variant
  - redwood_ext_<name>_processing_seconds_bucket shows increased tail
  - kernel-scheduler-service queue_length metric increases > 2x baseline

- Immediate actions (pager):
  1) If invocation_errors_total rate > 0.5% over 1 minute: trigger rollback and page oncall (eng-sre).
  2) If latency_p95 breached threshold by >20% for 5 minutes: toggle routing in kernel-scheduler-service to fallback variant: curl -X POST https://kernel-scheduler.internal/_admin/fallback?variant=cpu-fallback
  3) Temporarily isolate the extension by marking it non-preferred: runtime-orchestrator API: POST /extensions/<name>/isolate
  4) Capture a 2-minute profiler run and attach ext.name tag, then escalate to runtime team.

Post-incident triage checklist
- Collect: perf-harness-runner results, OTLP traces for the period, Prometheus metrics (10m before/after), kernel dispatcher logs, kv-cache-agent metrics.
- Hypothesis-driven triage steps: check for memory growth in extension, kernel preemption events, unexpected concurrency spikes, network stalls on telemetry-pipeline.
- RCA artifacts: timeline, root-cause hypothesis, corrective change, and automated gate added to CI (if applicable).

Known integration pitfalls and recommended mitigations
| Issue | Likely cause | Recommended mitigation |
|-------|--------------|------------------------|
| Unbounded worker spawn | Extension ignores resources field on manifest | Reject manifest on validation; implement soft cgroups limits and autoscale advisory |
| Kernel preemption thrash | Long-running kernels without cooperative yield | Add cooperative yield hooks; break kernels into smaller micro-kernels |
| KV cache stampede | Extension performs cold synchronous cache fills | Use async prefetch; set max_prefetch_inflight=4; use per-tenant rate limit |
| OTLP flooding | Excessive debug-level spans from extension | Require sampling controls and log-level thresholds; telemetry-pipeline enforces rate limits |

Appendix A: Example Prometheus metric exposition (text-format)
# HELP redwood_ext_fast_attn_invocations_total Total invocations to fast-attn extension
# TYPE redwood_ext_fast_attn_invocations_total counter
redwood_ext_fast_attn_invocations_total{status="ok",node="node-az1-07"} 12345

# HELP redwood_ext_fast_attn_processing_seconds Histogram of processing durations in seconds
# TYPE redwood_ext_fast_attn_processing_seconds histogram
redwood_ext_fast_attn_processing_seconds_bucket{le="0.01"} 1000
redwood_ext_fast_attn_processing_seconds_bucket{le="0.05"} 12000

Appendix B: Minimal extension SDK checklist (for authors)
- Implement /healthz and /ready endpoints
- Emit the required metrics with correct naming
- Register shapes via RegisterExtension before accepting requests
- Honor resources settings and implement graceful shutdown hooks
- Provide a benchmark_profile and test vectors in the manifest

Related artifacts and links

- Kernel scheduler admin API: https://kernel-scheduler.internal/_admin

If you are integrating a third-party extension, file a request in the #runtime-extensions slack channel and follow the vendor-onboarding runbook referenced from the registry UI.
